title: Relating material experience to technical parameters: A case study on visual and tactile warmth perception of indoor wall materials
research_question: To what extent can the experience of material warmth be described in relation to technical material parameters, specifically for indoor wall materials? This includes investigating: a) the contribution of vision and touch to warmth perception, b) relationships between material warmth and technical material parameters, and c) the effect of non-color material parameters compared to material color on warmth perception.

participants.description: 116 unpaid volunteers (60 female, 56 male), undergraduate and graduate students in Architectural Engineering of the Vrije Universiteit Brussel (VUB), aged 17-25 (mean 21).

stimuli_or_exposures.description: 11 physical material samples (0.4m x 0.4m) presented vertically at eye-height in white mdf-cases. This included 6 original building materials (blue stone, brickwork, concrete, white plaster, steel, wood) and 5 colored plaster control samples matching the colors of the original materials.

mechanisms: The visual modality attracts significant attention, potentially distracting from other sensory perceptions.
People's visual assessment of material warmth is influenced by their prior tactile knowledge and associations (e.g., wood feels warm, steel feels cold).
The interrelationship between gloss and roughness may contribute to the tactile perception of gloss.
Multisensory perception of warmth for 'cold-warm' is dominated by vision.
Material properties (thermal, surface) and color contribute to warmth perception, with color having a larger effect.
implementation_implications: Architects should distinguish between visual and tactile warmth to be more aware of different sensory inputs in design.
Material databases should include technical parameters like thermal effusivity and surface gloss, along with tactile and visual warmth indications, to inform material selection.
Architects can influence warmth experience by considering materials with high thermal effusivity, warm colors, and low glossiness.
Architects can use different finishing techniques to manipulate surface gloss and thus the experience of warmth.
Applying color to a material is a more effective way to alter warmth perception than changing surface roughness or gloss.

tables.description: Overview of thermal properties and technical measurements of the test samples (Blue stone, Brickwork, Concrete, Plaster, Steel, Wood). Includes thermal conductivity, specific heat, density, thermal effusivity, average roughness Ra, mean square roughness Rq, gloss (60° and 85°), lightness L*, red-green value a*, yellow-blue value b*, and color intensity I*.
Pearson correlation coefficients between evaluated material warmth and physical measures in the three experimental conditions (General, Visual, Tactile).

limitations: The limited variety of materials (6 original, 5 plaster) did not allow for detailed findings on exact relationships between warmth and technical parameters.
The material set and researched variables (thermal properties, surface roughness, gloss) need to be expanded and controlled for generalization.
The sample set for colors was not chosen to cover a wide variety, requiring caution in interpreting color results.
The study focused on indoor wall materials, and warmth perception is context-dependent, so results may not generalize to other building elements (floors, ceilings) or outdoor applications.
Participants were asked to imagine materials at full scale, but their ability to do so might be limited, potentially affecting perception.
